title: A Room for the Visitor
premise: Jude Ishikawa, a meticulous pest controller who treats documentation as ritual, is called to Marrow House, where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed walls. As Jude documents, every mirror in the house begins reflecting rooms one second late—and in that stolen second, Jude sees themselves doing things they haven't done yet. The house's last resident, elderly Ada Voss, is preparing to sign the property over to a development firm, and the entity's grip strengthens as the papers near completion. Jude discovers that in 1974 Ada took something from the thing in the walls—her sister's name, spoken into a jar and buried—and only by returning it can anyone leave whole. In the end, Jude convinces Ada to dig up and unseal the jar at the moment of signing; the name returns to its owner, the mirrors catch up to real time, and Jude walks out changed: visible, documented, and finally belonging to themselves.
about_author: Beatrix Oyelaran is a former building inspector from Lagos and Leeds whose horror fiction grew out of years of surveying houses that refused to behave like houses. She writes in the margins of structural reports and believes every haunting is a paperwork problem.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Jude Ishikawa, who arrives at Marrow House for a routine infestation complaint and finds claw-shaped fingerprints pressed into plaster behind a sealed wall. Jude photographs everything, cataloguing compulsively. The emotional beat is professional calm stretched over unease—the first crack in Jude's belief that observation keeps them safe.

chapters.title: Ada Voss Signs Nothing Yet
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Ada, 81, alone in the house she refuses to sell, rehearsing her signature for the developer's papers. She hears her sister Ruth's voice in the skirting boards. The beat is stubborn grief: Ada knows what lives here and has decided to die negotiating.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Back with Jude, who notices the hallway mirror reflecting their movements a full second behind. They test it scientifically—timers, video—until the reflection waves when they don't. The beat is the collapse of rational method; documentation becomes prayer because nothing else works.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Wrongs
chapters.summary: Jude interviews neighbors and finds a pattern: everyone who lived at Marrow House lost something small—a name misspelled on a deed, a face missing from a photo. POV alternates between Jude's field notes and a 1974 newspaper clipping. The beat is dread accumulating through bureaucracy.

chapters.title: What the Walls Kept
chapters.summary: Ada, POV, remembers 1974: Ruth dying, and Ada speaking Ruth's name into a glass jar and burying it beneath the floorboards so death couldn't take all of her. Something answered from the walls. The beat is guilt dressed up as love.

chapters.title: The Second Visitor
chapters.summary: Jude returns after hours, unable to stay away, and meets another figure in the upstairs mirror—one second ahead now, wearing Jude's coat. It signs Jude's name in the dust. The beat is identity horror: the reflection is applying for Jude's life.

chapters.title: Papers of Record
chapters.summary: The developer's lawyer, Mr. Okonjo, arrives with final sale documents; Ada stalls, claiming a missing signature from a dead man. Jude, hired officially to 'clear' the house, realizes the signing date is a deadline for something older than real estate. Beat: two kinds of paperwork, both predatory.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Jude matches the wall prints to their own hands—slightly larger, slightly wrong. They stop sleeping, start recording audio, and capture a second voice under their own narration, correcting their words. Beat: the terror of being edited.

chapters.title: Ruth, Briefly
chapters.summary: A short chapter in the voice of whatever answers to Ruth's name, half-awake in the walls, feeling itself be remembered incorrectly. It wants its name back but has forgotten what it was for. Beat: monstrous sympathy—the entity is also a victim of theft.

chapters.title: The Jar
chapters.summary: Jude finds Ada digging at the floorboards at 3 a.m., bare-handed, and stops her: the floor above the burial site is warm and breathing. Ada confesses everything about 1974. Beat: alliance formed between the documenter and the thief.

chapters.title: Mirror Work
chapters.summary: Jude covers every mirror in black plastic; the reflections migrate to windows, water, Jude's phone screen. The lag becomes two seconds, then three, and the other Jude starts arriving before Jude does. Beat: losing the race to yourself.

chapters.title: Okonjo's Second Visit
chapters.summary: The lawyer pushes the signing to Friday, revealing he's been coming to this house for decades without aging a day—he sold it once before, in 1974, to the Voss sisters. Beat: the corruption of power; the sale is how the house feeds.

chapters.title: Everything Documented
chapters.summary: Jude reviews their own footage and finds scenes they never filmed: themselves standing over Ada's bed, opening the floorboards, smiling. The record no longer distinguishes Jude from the visitor. Beat: despair—evidence indicts the innocent.

chapters.title: The Name in the Jar
chapters.summary: Ada tells Jude the rule she learned too late: a name kept is a person kept, and a person kept belongs to the keeper—but the walls have been keeping HER, not Ruth, all these years. Beat: revelation reframing the entire haunting.

chapters.title: Invisible Was a Choice
chapters.summary: Jude confronts their own history—years of making themselves small, unphotographed, unlisted—and realizes the house chose them precisely because they practiced disappearance. The reflection offers Jude permanence in exchange for stepping aside. Beat: temptation articulated as belonging.

chapters.title: Friday
chapters.summary: Signing day. Okonjo arrives with witnesses who cast no shadows; Ada sits with the pen untouched while the walls sweat and the mirrors run four seconds late. Jude cuts the power and the house keeps humming anyway. Beat: held breath before the climax.

chapters.title: Unsealing
chapters.summary: Climax part one: Ada and Jude pry up the boards together while the house fights back—doors sealing, prints crawling across skin, the other Jude stepping out of the hall mirror to sign the papers in Jude's stead. Beat: physical struggle between two claimants to one life.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Climax part two: Ada opens the jar and speaks Ruth's true full name—not the one she buried, but the one Ruth chose for herself, which Ada had never used. The name leaves the jar, the walls exhale, and the reflection collapses back into ordinary glass. Beat: restitution as exorcism.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: With the entity released, Ada signs the papers freely—or tears them up; she chooses to will the house to the town as a memorial to Ruth. Okonjo ages forty years in the doorway and leaves without his commission. Beat: power dissolved by an act of ownership freely given.

chapters.title: Afterimage
chapters.summary: Jude, POV, walks the emptied house documenting the aftermath: clean mirrors, cold walls, one set of fingerprints that are unmistakably their own and exactly the right size. They file the report honestly, including everything they almost did. Beat: quiet reckoning.

chapters.title: A Room for the Visitor
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Jude keeps a single room in their own apartment bare—unfurnished, unphotographed—as a courtesy to whatever might visit, having learned the difference between hiding and hosting. A knock comes; Jude opens the door. Beat: transformed fear into hospitality.

chapters.title: Appendix: Field Notes, Annotated
chapters.summary: Epistolary coda: Jude's case file reproduced with marginalia in a second handwriting that is also theirs, dated after the events, agreeing with every line. The final note reads: 'Documented. Belonging to myself.' Beat: resolution with a resonant, open hum.
